title: Shakti as a philosophy
hook: a poet about to write a long poem asks for one thing first: that his words and their meanings stay together

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Devi Upanishad: the gods asked who are you, and the goddess answered, of the nature of Brahman.

A poet sits down to write a long poem about the kings of Raghu's line, one king after another. And the first thing he writes isn't about any king. It's about a word and its meaning. The poet is Kalidasa, whose Parvati this path met in the forest not long ago. Before he tells a single story, he bows to a couple. Not a king and queen: Shiva and Parvati. And he chooses one picture to say how close they are.
screen: `A LONG POEM OF KINGS.` → `FIRST: A WORD AND ITS MEANING.` → `HE BOWS TO A COUPLE.`

segments.voice: Here is the verse, in paraphrase. Joined like word and meaning, for the sake of understanding word and meaning, I bow to the parents of the world, Parvati and Shiva. First, the picture. Word and meaning aren't two things that happen to be in the same room. A word without meaning is just noise. A meaning needs some sign to carry it. They are two, and they are never apart. That's how close the poet says the goddess and the god are. Second, why he asks. He bows to them for the sake of understanding word and meaning. He's about to spend a whole poem putting words to work, so he asks the couple who are word and meaning to help his words mean something. It's a writer's prayer, and a clever one: the same image twice, once about God and once about his craft. Third, the parents of the world. Kalidasa doesn't call Parvati a helper or a shadow. Mother and father together are where the world comes from. That fits this week: Shiva can't stir without Shakti; Uma names Brahman; nature and spirit both come from the goddess. Fourth, the image people know. In temples and paintings, Shiva and Parvati are sometimes shown as one body, half him and half her, divided down the middle: Ardhanarishvara, the lord who is half woman. The poet's word and meaning and the sculptor's single body say the same thing in two arts. In both pictures, Shakti isn't a second god beside the first. She's the other half of the same one.
screen: `JOINED LIKE WORD AND MEANING.` · `A WRITER'S PRAYER, TWICE OVER.` · `THE PARENTS OF THE WORLD.` · `ONE BODY: HALF SHIVA, HALF PARVATI.` · then, large: `TWO, AND NEVER APART.`

segments.voice: Choose one simple word that matters to you, home, mother, peace, a name, and say it once, silently, then watch what arrives with it: a picture, a feeling, a face. Say it again, slowly, and rest wherever the sound and the sense meet. If you pray, you can choose the name of the goddess, or Shiva, or the name you use for God.
Shakti as a philosophy. Kalidasa bows to Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, joined like a word and its meaning.
Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. Two, like a word and its meaning, and never apart. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The opening verse of Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha is learned by students of Sanskrit and recited as an invocation, and images of Ardhanarishvara, half Shiva and half Parvati, stand in temples dedicated to Shiva.

chat.says: Why does Kalidasa compare Shiva and Parvati to a word and its meaning?
options: Because they're two and never apart: a word needs meaning, and meaning needs a word.
Because Parvati is the word and only repeats whatever Shiva, the meaning, decides.
Because the poet wanted a neat rhyme, and the comparison has no deeper point.
chat.meaning: The Raghuvamsha's first verse bows to Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, joined like word and meaning: two, and never apart.

Raghu.meaning: an ancestor-king whose line the long poem follows

Parvati.meaning: the goddess, Shiva's wife; here a parent of the world

Ardhanarishvara.meaning: Shiva and Parvati shown as one body, half and half

notes: Raghuvamsha 1.1 paraphrased: vāgarthāv iva saṃpṛktau vāgarthapratipattaye / jagataḥ pitarau vande pārvatīparameśvarau. 'Parameshvara' given as Shiva.
Kalidasa is called only 'a poet of classical Sanskrit' to avoid superlatives and dates.
Ardhanarishvara is not in the cited verse; it is a general description of the image. 'Half woman' for ardha-nārī is a gloss of the name; confirm acceptable under the etymology rule.
howItsDone's claim that Ardhanarishvara images stand in Shiva temples is general; Keeper to confirm.
